title: Fifty Years of Southern Resident Killer Whale Research: Scientific Discoveries to Conservation Crises
content:
ABSTRACT

The long-term study of the southern resident killer whales (SRKWs) (Orcinus orca ater) in the northeastern Pacific Ocean represents one of the longest-running and most comprehensive individual-based studies of any marine mammal. In 2026, the Orca Survey Project—the long-term behavioral and demographic study of the SRKW population conducted by the Center for Whale Research—marks its 50th anniversary. Here we synthesize five decades of research by the international community studying the southern resident killer whales. We revisit the pioneering work that first enabled individual killer whales to be identified through their unique markings, laying the foundation for discoveries about their life histories, complex social structure, and relationships. We further explore changes in habitat use and prey ecology over recent decades, and how emerging technologies are transforming our understanding of the population. Intensive study over the last 50 years has revealed this population remains at critical risk of extinction. We review the principal threats to the population, including disease, noise disturbance, pollution, inbreeding, and declining prey availability. When taken together, this body of work underscores the value of sustained individual-based studies for understanding the evolution, behavior, and conservation of long-lived marine mammals.
